# A hybrid machine learning and physics-based approach to model high-resolution inundation

Amelia Peeples a,∗iD, Elena Leonarduzzi b, Laura E. Condon c, Reed M. Maxwell a,∗iD

a Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA b Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research WSL, Birmensdorf, Switzerland c Department of Hydrology and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA

H I G H L I G H T S

• Predicts high-resolution inundation by using machine learning to downscale a hydrologic model. • Achieves high accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost of physics-based modeling alone. • Maintains high accuracy in locations and time periods excluded from training data.

A R T I C L E  I N F O

This manuscript was handled by the assistance of Ashok Mishra, Associate Editor

Keywords: Random forest Machine learning ParFlow-CLM Hydrologic model Downscaling Surface water

A B S T R A C T

Large-scale high-resolution hydrologic modeling is necessary to understand future water availability and flood risk. This study uses a combined physics-based and machine learning modeling approach to produce accurate high-resolution inundation maps at a much lower computational cost than high-resolution physics-based mod­ eling. The test domain is an 1800 km2 watershed in Colorado during the 2019 water year which is modeled in the integrated surface-subsurface model ParFlow-CLM at a 1 km resolution and then downscaled to a 100 m resolution binary inundation product using a random forest model. In addition to the 1 km resolution modeled inundation depth, other relevant parameters such as topographic slope, upstream area, and Manning’s rough­ ness are inputs for the machine learning model. The random forest model was trained on a synthetic ground truth modeled by a 100 m resolution ParFlow-CLM model. The hybrid physics-based and machine learning ap­ proach is 97.6% accurate (F1 score of 0.96) in predicting high-resolution inundation status when compared to the 100 m resolution ParFlow-CLM model at 1/500th of the computational cost. This is more accurate than the 1 km model on its own, which is 67.4% accurate at a 100 m resolution. Even when only considering locations with temporally-variable inundation, the hybrid model is 93.6% accurate (F1 score of 0.91). The performance of the hybrid methodology given incomplete spatial or temporal training data was also tested and it was found that the model is 96.2% accurate in unseen timesteps and 86.4% accurate in unseen locations (F1 scores of 0.94 and 0.75 respectively). This study demonstrates the applicability of a hybrid physics-based and machine learning approach to produce accurate high-resolution surface inundation maps at a dramatically lower computational cost than high-resolution hydrologic modeling.

## 1 . Introduction

Creating “everywhere and locally relevant” (Bierkens et al., 2015) hydrologic models has been a longstanding goal in the field of hydrol­ ogy. There have been many studies creating large-scale “hyperresolu­ tion” hydrologic models (David et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2023; Cosgrove et al., 2024) but even at the highest resolution of 1 km, they are still too coarse for many applications. The computational expense associated

with large-scale high-resolution hydrologic models has led to the use of other methodologies, such as machine learning (ML), to try to produce large-scale, high-resolution surface water data. Remotely sensed satellite data have also been used to produce high-resolution surface data prod­ ucts (Pekel et al., 2016; Klein et al., 2024), which can be used on their own or as reference data for modeling methodologies. Satellite-based methods have the advantage of global coverage at high-resolutions but

also have the disadvantages of infrequent flyover times, meaning they might not capture all extreme events, as well as the inability to predict future events. There is a need for large-scale high-resolution hydro­ logic models to understand future water availability and flood risk, but high-resolution physics-based modeling is prohibitively expensive for continental or global-scale applications.

In recent years, there have been many studies applying ML meth­ ods to surface hydrology. Some examples include using ML to predict channel flow (Booker and Woods, 2014; Bhusal et al., 2022; Schoppa et al., 2020; Shahariar et al., 2026) and classify flood risk (Wang et al., 2015; Woznicki et al., 2019). Other studies have also attempted to use ML models as surrogates or emulators for physics-based modeling due to the fast computational speeds and ability to closely match model out­ puts (Maxwell et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020; Zahura et al., 2020; Tran et al., 2021). Many of these studies use physics-based models to produce training data, but do not use physics-based modeling as a part of their predictions. More recently, there have also been hybrid modeling ap­ proaches combining both machine learning and physics-based modeling together in workflows. Hydrologic models and machine learning models have been applied in series, such as by coupling a random forest model and a hydrologic model to predict whether intermittent river reaches would be wet or dry (Mimeau et al., 2024), by inputting flows predicted by a random forest model into a hydraulic model to simulate water depth (Bhusal et al., 2022), and by correcting modeled streamflow using a machine learning post-processing step (Solanki et al., 2025). Machine learning approaches have also been incorporated directly into hydro­ logic models to improve accuracy of modeling surface flows (Feng et al., 2023; Bindas et al., 2024; Huynh et al., 2025). While hybrid machine learning and physics-based approaches are becoming more common in surface water modeling, they are nearly always used to model stream­ flow or surface flow. Applying these hybrid methodologies to directly model inundated areas has been much less explored.

Concurrently, ML methods have also become more common in down­ scaling climate and hydrological variables from satellite data. Surface temperature (Hutengs and Vohland, 2016), precipitation (Chen et al., 2021, 2024), water storage anomaly (Kalu et al., 2024; Rostami Khalaj et al., 2026), and soil moisture (Vergopolan et al., 2021) have all been downscaled from coarse satellite data to higher-resolution products us­ ing ML methods. ML has also been used to downscale satellite-based surface inundation (Nguyen and Aires, 2024; Wu and Liu, 2015; Yue et al., 2023) and river width (Ling et al., 2019). In addition to downscaling satellite data, ML methods have also recently been used to downscale cli­ mate model outputs (Lin et al., 2023; Rampal et al., 2022; Lopez-Gomez et al., 2025). Applying a similar approach of using ML to downscale surface water products produced by physics-based models could poten­ tially bypass the prohibitively high cost of large-scale high-resolution hydrologic modeling.

The problem of downscaling modeled surface water is not a new one, although it has not been the focus of many studies. Schumann et al. (2014) first proposed downscaling as a potential solution to the is­ sue of the impossible cost of high-resolution modeling at large scales.

They proposed a post-processing methodology to increase resolution in and around floodplains and found success in downscaling a 600m resolution LISFLOOD model to produce 30m resolution surface water depths. Bryant et al. (2024) later proposed a downscaling methodology based on bilinear resampling to be applied to coarse modeled inun­ dation as a more efficient and comparably accurate replacement for high-resolution modeling. While several methodologies exist to pro­ cess coarse-resolution inundation produced from hydrologic models into higher-resolution inundation products, these methods rely on direct in­ terpolation or terrain-based refinement and cannot capture the actual hydrology at a higher resolution than the input model. Inundation down­ scaling is a good potential application of machine learning as it is able to learn more complex relationships between a coarse model and highresolution inundation while being much more computationally efficient than increasing model resolution. This has been done before with 1D inundation depth within a channel using a physics-informed neural net­ work (Feng et al., 2023). More recently this has also been done to downscale 2D modeled urban flood inundation (Choi et al., 2025) and flood probability maps (Huang et al., 2025). This study builds on these previous works by applying hybrid physics-based and ML approaches to predict 2D inundation with the aim of capturing seasonal expansion and contraction of large rivers as opposed to flood events over shorter time frames.

The aim of this study is to propose and test a hybrid methodology to predict high-resolution surface inundation presence accurately and efficiently by combining coarse-resolution physics-based modeling and machine learning-based downscaling. In this work, a Random Forest model is used to downscale modeled surface inundation from the model resolution of 1 km to 100 m. Tree-based ML methods, such as Random Forest (RF) models (Breiman, 2001), have previously been successful in downscaling satellite data (Hutengs and Vohland, 2016) as well as fill­ ing in gaps between point measurements (Ma et al., 2024a,b; Chang et al., 2024; Goodling et al., 2024). While other ML methods which explic­ itly respect spatial or temporal relationships could also be used, an RF model was selected due to its simplicity, explainability, and flexibility with sparse noncontinuous and nonsequential training data. This study is similar to Mimeau et al. (2024) but rather than predicting whether river reaches will be inundated daily, a 2D spatial array of inundation status is predicted across the entire model domain hourly. It is also sim­ ilar to Choi et al. (2025) but aims to capture changes in inundation over larger timescales than urban flood events. Fig. 1 shows a conceptual overview of this coupled physics-based and ML modeling process. The accuracy of the hybrid model is assessed by comparing its predicted in­ undation to modeled inundation from the 100 m ParFlow-CLM model. The model’s accuracy when applied to completely unseen timesteps and unseen locations within the same domain is also evaluated.

First, a coarse-resolution (1 km) ParFlow-CLM inte­ grated hydrologic model was run for the time period and location of interest to produce 1 km resolution modeled pressure head at the ground surface for each hourly timestep. Next, the modeled pressure head data were combined with nine additional inputs. If an input’s spatial resolu­ tion was coarser than the 100 m target resolution, it was homogeneously resampled to a 100 m resolution. Each data point corresponds to one high-resolution cell at one timestep and the associated value of each of the ten input parameters. All ten input parameters, their sources, and their starting resolutions are described in Table 1. Most of these input pa­ rameters are static, such as upstream area and Manning’s roughness, but modeled pressure head, temperature, and precipitation are temporallydependent. Finally, each data point was fed into a random forest model that predicts binary inundation status (wet or dry) for that cell at that timestep. The random forest model was trained on high-resolution bi­ nary inundation data produced by a 100 m resolution ParFlow-CLM model run over the same spatial domain for the same time period, which was also used to determine the accuracy of this downscaling approach. The final output is 100 m hourly binary inundation status. By starting with a 1 km resolution hydrologic model, this methodology ensures that mass is conserved at the 1 km resolution. While the RF model is unable to guarantee mass is conserved at the 100 m resolution, this is mitigated by predicting inundation status directly rather than predicting volume or flux at the 100 m resolution.

This methodology is applied to the East-Taylor Watershed in Colorado, USA over the full 2019 water year using modeled inundation as training data. The East-Taylor Watershed is a HUC8 watershed and is approximately 1800 km2. Much of the streamflow in this watershed is groundwater- and snowmelt-fed, leading to a strong seasonal pattern in its surface flow. This strong dependence on snow and groundwater necessitates a hydrologic model which models land surface, surface, and subsurface processes together, which is very computationally expensive and highlights the need for a more efficient alternative to high-resolution modeling. The inundation data produced for this watershed is modeled based on the real-world input datasets but was not validated against ob­ served inundation and should be regarded as a synthetic ground truth as opposed to an accurate representation of inundation in this watershed.

2.1 . Hydrologic models

2.1.1 . Coarse-resolution ParFlow-CLM model

ParFlow-CLM (PF-CLM) is an integrated surface-subsurface model coupled with a land surface model and can run efficiently at large scales (Ashby and Falgout, 1996; Jones and Woodward, 2001; Kollet and Maxwell, 2006; Maxwell, 2013; Maxwell and Miller, 2005; Kollet and Maxwell, 2008). The 1 km resolution model was subset directly from the CONUS2 PF-CLM model and was validated against real-world

observations including streamflow (Yang et al., 2023). The atmospheric forcing inputs, such as precipitation and temperature, were updated to CW3E data (CW3E, 2024) retrieved from HydroData (Defnet et al., 2024; Triplett et al., 2024). Three total years of forcing data from the 2019 wa­ ter year were run in succession to spin up the model to this new forcing dataset. The model was considered to be adequately spun up for the purposes of this study since annual outflow and surface water storage did not change significantly across simulation years. This model takes approximately 30min on 16 CPUs to run one year of hourly computa­ tions and has 1890 surface cells within its domain (18,900 cells total including subsurface cells).

2.1.2 . High-resolution modeled reference data

The 100 m PF-CLM model was created by homogeneously resampling all inputs except slopes from the CONUS2 PF-CLM model to a 100 m resolution. A 30m DEM (NASA, 2019) was resampled to a 100 m resolu­ tion and then processed using the PriorityFlow R package (Condon and Maxwell, 2019) to determine the high-resolution watershed boundary and slopes in both the x- and y-directions for each cell. While this model was not explicitly validated, all inputs besides the high-resolution slopes were taken directly from the validated CONUS2 PF-CLM model. This model was spun up by running four years of the 2019 water year forc­ ing data based on the same criteria described above. This model takes approximately 24 hours on 384 CPUs to run one year of hourly com­ putations and has 187,576 surface cells within its domain (1,875,760 cells total). The output inundation from this model is used as a synthetic ground truth, which is further discussed in Section 2.2.1.

2.2 . Baseline random forest model

The goal of the RF model is to downscale modeled binary inundation status (wet vs. dry) from 1 km to 100 m resolution. To do this, a classi­ fication RF model was developed to take in the modeled 1 km pressure head output at the ground surface homogeneously resampled to a 100 m resolution along with nine other hydrologically relevant parameters and predict the inundation status of each 100 m cell independently at each timestep. A list of input parameters can be found in Table 1.

The classification RF model was developed using scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011). Approximately 2.5% of the data (40 million points) was used for training. Larger training datasets were tested but had marginal impacts on accuracy while greatly increasing computa­ tional cost. Additionally, using a very limited training dataset provides useful information on the accuracy of this methodology with sparse training data. Half of the training data points were inundated and half were not inundated, but otherwise the training data was randomly se­ lected from the full dataset. This means no time steps or spatial locations were held out when training the baseline RF model. The training data

2.2.1 . Rationale for training on modeled inundation

It is important to highlight that the RF models in this study were trained and validated on modeled inundation data produced by the highresolution PF-CLM model and were not validated against real-world inundation data. Any inaccuracies present in the 100 m PF-CLM modeled inundation will be propagated into the RF model but for the purposes of this study, the 100 m modeled inundation is treated as a synthetic ground truth.

Training and validating on modeled inundation serves two purposes. First, since hydrologic models are widely used to predict inundation, a methodology that produces these inundation predictions at a lower computational cost and is accurate compared to an existing model is valuable in itself. Second, by intentionally limiting training data, using modeled training data allows controlled exploration into the amount of training data required to produce accurate high-resolution inundation predictions and into how prediction quality is impacted by limited spa­ tial and temporal coverage in training data. This study serves as a proof of concept for the applicability of this methodology to be trained on sparse data, such as satellite-observed water presence.

2.3 . Temporal and spatial ablation models

Two additional RF-PF models were created to test the performance of this methodology on completely unseen timesteps and locations within the same spatial and temporal domain as other training data. This is to rigorously test the applicability of this methodology when available training data are sparse, such as the incomplete and infrequent observa­ tions produced by satellite remote sensing. The impact of withholding spatial and temporal information was independently tested to explore potential model degradation during unobserved times in between passes as well as in locations which are either never seen or lack high quality observations.

The temporal and spatial ablation RF-PF models are identical to the baseline RF-PF model except that they were trained on different subsets of the full dataset. Rather than training on data randomly se­ lected from the entire dataset, roughly half of the data was held out, either spatially or temporally, and not randomly sampled for training. The accuracy of these ablation models applied to the unseen data sub­ sets can be compared to the baseline RF-PF model to assess the loss in accuracy associated with completely unseen times or locations and de­ termine if this methodology is robust given incomplete training data and is generalizable within the same watershed.

2.3.1 . Temporal ablation RF-PF model

To test performance on completely unseen timesteps, the temporal domain of one water year was split into nine 1000 hr slices (the last one being 760 hr). Alternating slices were used as the training domain (4760 hr total) and were held out to evaluate model performance (4000 hr total). 40 million data points were randomly selected from the training domain to train a new RF-PF model. The accuracy of this hybrid method­ ology in unseen timesteps can then be determined by using the temporal ablation RF-PF to predict inundation during the held out timesteps. It is important to note that more than half of the peak snowmelt period was held out from training. While this isn’t an independent event, it does allow analysis of model performance during extreme events.

2.3.2 . Spatial ablation RF-PF model

To test performance on unseen locations within a known domain the spatial domain was split into seven 10 km slices (the last one being 8 km). These slices span the full latitude of the domain and 10 km of the longitude each. Alternating slices were used as the training domain (four slices) and were held out to evaluate model performance (three slices). Despite being different numbers of slices, these two domains are roughly equal in size. 40 million data points were randomly selected from the training domain to train a new RF-PF model. The accuracy of this hybrid methodology in unseen locations can then be determined by using the spatial ablation RF-PF to predict inundation in the held out locations.

3.2.1 . Accuracy in variably inundated cells

During the 2019 water year, 14.9% of the spatial domain was always inundated and 48.1% was never inundated. Only the remaining 37.0% of cells had temporally-variable inundation. Since just over a third of cells had temporally-variable inundation, a model could appear to have a high predictive accuracy by always predicting the most likely status of each cell without capturing any of the temporal dynamics of the system. To account for this, the predictive accuracy was also computed only in variably inundated cells.

The baseline RF-PF model is accurate in 93.6% of predictions in cells which are variably inundated and has an F1 score of 0.91 (Table 2). This is lower than the overall accuracy of the model, but is still a very high predictive accuracy. Fig. 7 shows the relationship between model accuracy and temporal variability in inundation status. ## 4 . Discussion

4.1 . Identifying areas for improvement in baseline RF-PF model

Overall, the baseline RF-PF model accurately captures both spatial patterns and temporal patterns. While it is still generally accurate in cells with high temporal variability (Fig. 7), predictions in these cells are still systematically less accurate than the average. This can also be seen when comparing areas of lower accuracy in Fig. 6(A) to areas with more variable inundation in Fig. 6(B). While the accuracy in these cells is still generally high, it is lower than the average predictive accuracy of the model. The accuracy in these highly variable cells should be improved to increase the utility of this hybrid modeling approach. This section will identify areas where accuracy could be improved and suggest potential future solutions.

4.1.1 . Headwaters during snowmelt

The baseline RF-PF model predicts a higher rate of inundation during peak snowmelt than the 100 m PF-CLM model (Fig. 3). This is primarily due to overestimation of the extent of seasonal inundation surrounding headwater streams (Fig. 4). Most cells which have temporally variable inundation will be inundated during the summer months, as that is when snowmelt leads to seasonal streams containing water and increasing flow in permanent rivers. Despite being a very hydrologically significant time, the season when snowmelt is driving flow is a relatively small portion of the year. Therefore, since training data was randomly sampled through­ out the water year, a small portion of training data came from timesteps during snowmelt. It was found during model development that training the RF model on a higher proportion of inundated cells improved model accuracy so future studies should test if including a higher proportion of training data from timesteps where inundated area is high could further increase the predictive accuracy of this methodology.

The hybrid model’s performance during snowmelt, despite snowmelt being annually recurring, is an extreme event within the context of one year of data and can be used to infer the model’s accuracy when predict­ ing less frequent extreme events, such as flooding. As would be expected, the baseline RF-PF model had lower accuracy when inundated area was at the maximum inundated area that was included in the training data but it still produced physically reasonable inundation predictions.

The overall accuracy of the baseline RF-PF model is also lower than would be explained only by the overestimation of inundated area, mean­ ing there are other areas of underestimating inundation during this time period (Fig. 5). The baseline RF-PF model only overestimated inundated area by 1–2% but inaccurately predicted inundation status by up to 10% during this time, meaning the model was very accurate at predicting how much inundation there should be and a bit less accurate at predicting which cells specifically were inundated. This could be because the cells surrounding headwater streams had very similar physical characteris­ tics but whether or not they were inundated was related to the physical distribution of the snowpack, which is not known by the random forest model. The snowpack is modeled by the 1 km resolution PF-CLM model and is relevant in producing the 1 km resolution pressure head input, but including the snowpack as a spatially and temporally-variable input into the RF model could help increase accuracy.

In addition, there are no 100 m resolution temporally-variable inputs to the RF model, so all temporal variability is only at the 1 km resolu­ tion. The most important temporally-variable feature for the Random Forest model is the 1 km modeled pressure head (Table 1). Therefore, most of the temporal variability for each 100 m cell will be based on the temporal variability of the inundation in the 1 km PF-CLM cell it falls within. In many cases, 1 km-scale temporal variability may not be rep­ resentative of temporal variability at the 100 m scale. For example, in a 1 km cell that contains a stream, the 100 m cells which are outside of that stream but fall within the same 1 km cell may have different pat­ terns of temporal variability than the stream and those patterns will not be captured within the input data to the RF-PF model. The accuracy of the baseline RF-PF model could be increased by adding 100 m resolution temporal inputs.

Separating the downscaling methodology into two steps, such as predicting or sup­ plying a static inundation map and then predicting temporal anomalies from that map, could help more accurately predict temporal variability.

4.1.3 . High feature importance of static inputs

Analyzing feature importance allows better understanding of the drivers of model behavior. A successful downscaling model will learn the relationship between the coarse resolution inundation and the high resolution inundation. It is reasonable that this relationship would be dependent on static parameters since the physical properties of a loca­ tion are the biggest predictors of whether that location is likely to ever be inundated. If the RF model were only provided static inputs, it could still predict a reasonable average inundation status map but could not produce temporally-variable inundation. Temporally-variable inputs are essential to predicting if a location is inundated at a specific timestep, but the temporally variable inputs on their own could not create a rea­ sonable prediction without any information about the physical location. It is important to note that there are no 100 m resolution temporallydependent parameters included in this study. It is therefore expected and reasonable that the most important inputs to the RF model are temporally-static.

The feature importance of modeled pressure head (0.0619) and up­ stream area (0.1323) can be used to further contextualize the high feature importance of static parameters. Permutation feature importance is based on how impactful changing a certain input value is on the accu­ racy of predictions. As mentioned previously, only 37.0% of cells have temporally-variable inundation at all. This means that in the majority of cells, inundation status can be predicted from static parameters alone and the coarse PF-CLM modeled pressure head or other temporal inputs are not necessary for an accurate prediction. Therefore, it is expected that changing the input value of upstream area, which will be highly correlated with locations which are always inundated, will be very im­ pactful on model accuracy while changing the input value of modeled pressure head will be impactful on accuracy in fewer cells and therefore less important on average. Further testing should be done to determine if the learned relationship between the coarse and high resolution models holds during extreme or out-of-range events and if this methodology is able to predict unseen statuses such as predicting a cell to be inundated which was never inundated in the training data.

4.3 . Assessing and improving hybrid model performance given sparse training data

The accuracy of the baseline RF-PF model showcases the accuracy of the hybrid physics-based and machine learning methodology in the best case scenario where training data is available throughout the spa­ tial and temporal domain of interest but not at every location for every timestep. The accuracy of the spatial and temporal ablation RF-PF mod­ els illustrates how this methodology would perform in more common scenarios where training data is available for a similar time period or a similar location but not for the temporal or spatial domain of interest. Assessing the accuracy of this methodology when it is applied to not just unseen data points but unseen temporal or spatial domains can help de­ fine the applicability of this hybrid methodology and identify potential improvements to further enhance accuracy.

The temporal ablation RF-PF model applied to unseen timesteps has a very small decrease in accuracy compared to the baseline RF-PF model but most of this decrease occurs in cells with high temporal variabil­ ity. This can be seen in Fig. 11 where the temporal ablation RF-PF model predicts more cells to be always inundated or never inundated than were modeled by the baseline RF-PF model or the 100 m PF-CLM

model. Despite this decrease in temporal variability, the spatial patterns are still well represented. This aligns with the dip in accuracy during peak flow when there is the most temporal variability in inundation status (Fig. 8). The temporal ablation RF-PF model was not trained on some of the most temporally variable timesteps in late spring and there­ fore it is not surprising that it has lower predictive accuracy in these timesteps and overall predicts lower temporal variability in inundation. When compared to the baseline RF-PF model and the spatial ablation RF-PF model, which were trained on data randomly selected from the full water year, the temporal ablation RF-PF model has a larger decrease in accuracy during peak flow relative to its accuracy during low flows. The accuracy of this methodology applied to unseen timesteps could be increased by training on a full water year of data before extrapolat­ ing outside of the temporal training domain to ensure that all seasonal dynamics are included in the training data.

The spatial ablation RF-PF model applied to unseen locations has a notable decrease in accuracy when compared to the baseline RF-PF model and it captures very little temporal variability in spatial cells out­ side of its training domain. This low temporal variability can be seen in Fig. 11 and is confirmed by the ‘X’ pattern in Fig. 10(B). There are still many cells which are modeled to have temporally variable inun­ dation but not nearly as many as are actually temporally variable in the 100 m PF-CLM model. The inputs to the RF model were not nor­ malized in a way that lends itself well to spatial generalizability even within the same domain. For example, elevation above sea level was an input in this study but elevation above nearest drainage or relative elevation compared to surrounding cells may result in a less domainspecific model. Future work using this methodology should test different ways to better normalize input data to improve the performance of this methodology in completely unseen locations. It is important to note that spatial generalizability was tested within the same HUC8 watershed as the training data. While these results do not show that this methodology is transferable to completely new spatial locations, they do suggest that this methodology can be used to fill in the gaps between observations in sparse inundation data.

4.4 . Real-world applications

While this study focused on the application of a hybrid ML and physics-based model to predict 100 m resolution inundation based on a 1 km resolution PF-CLM model, this methodology should be applica­ ble using different input hydrologic models at different spatial scales. This study proved this hybrid methodology to be applicable to increase resolution 100 times, but future research should explore the trade­ off between degree of resolution increase and accuracy. The following sections will describe proposed frameworks leveraging the very strong performance in unseen timesteps of this methodology to predict high resolution inundation.

4.4.1 . Substitute for high-resolution modeling to predict future inundation

The hybrid modeling methodology maintains high accuracy in un­ seen timesteps in a known spatial domain. After a high-resolution hydrologic model has been run for a short period of time to produce training data, the hybrid methodology could be used to model highresolution inundation over a longer time period or into the future. This is an improvement over forecasting at a lower resolution and produces a similar product to high resolution modeling at a much lower com­ putational cost. This low computational cost also makes it much more feasible to run large ensembles to account for uncertainty in forcing or static parameters, allowing the production of probabilistic inunda­ tion predictions at the same computational expense of deterministic inundation predictions from a high-resolution hydrologic model.

4.5 . Estimating confidence in predictions

The classification RF model consists of 50 trees which all indepen­ dently predict inundation status. Patterns in areas where there is strong agreement or disagreement between trees can be used to identify where the baseline RF-PF model may have higher or lower accuracy. There is a strong correlation between agreement among trees and RF model ac­ curacy in a spatial cell (SI Fig. 1). This means that the locations where there is a lot of disagreement between trees also have their inundation status incorrectly predicted more often than locations with minimal dis­ agreement between trees. In the context of using the outputs of this RF model to predict inundation area without a ground truth, the rate of agreement between trees can be used as a proxy for confidence in a given prediction.

4.6 . Computational efficiency

The goal of using a combined physics-based and ML modeling methodology is to produce high-resolution inundation maps with less computational cost than using a high-resolution physics-based model. The RF-PF model produced 100 m inundation predictions approximately 500 times faster than the high-resolution PF-CLM model with only a 2.4% decrease in accuracy. The 100 m PF-CLM model runs took approx­ imately 9216 core-hours (24 hours on 384 cores) to run one water year. The coarse PF-CLM model runs took approximately 8 core-hours (30min on 16 cores). The baseline RF model took approximately 10 core-hours (1.25 hours on 8 cores). Therefore, the combined PF-CLM and RF model approach to producing high-resolution inundation was approximately 500 times faster than running the high-resolution PF-CLM model.

Overall, this hybrid modeling approach is not only significantly faster than running a high resolution model but it can also be run in a reason­ able time on a fraction of the cores. The RF-PF model can be run on a typical four core personal computer to simulate one year of 100 m resolu­ tion hourly inundation for a watershed of similar size to the East-Taylor Watershed (1800 km2) in under five hours. Predicting the same inunda­ tion data on the same computer using a 100 m resolution PF-CLM model would take three months. This makes the RF-PF modeling methodol­ ogy much more accessible and applicable for real-world forecasting applications.

## 5 . Conclusions

This study demonstrates that a hybrid approach of machine learning and physics-based modeling can produce accurate high-resolution in­ undation predictions. A coarse (1 km) ParFlow-CLM model was used to produce surface water data which was downscaled using a random forest model to produce 100 m hourly inundation maps (together, the RF-PF model). Within the spatial and temporal training domain the baseline RF-PF model produces 97.6% accurate inundation predictions (F1 score of 0.96) when compared to a high-resolution physics-based model at 1/500th the computational cost. When excluding locations where inun­ dation is not temporally-variable, this hybrid model maintains a high accuracy of 93.6% (F1 score of 0.91).

The accuracy of this framework applied to times and locations not included in the training data was also assessed to evaluate the model’s robustness given sparse training data. Outside of the temporal training domain, the temporal ablation RF-PF model was 96.2% accurate in its inundation predictions (F1 score of 0.94), showing there is little decline

in accuracy when applying this methodology to unseen timesteps. The accuracy in only temporally-variable cells is also still high at 90.1% (F1 score of 0.87). These results support the applicability of this method­ ology to predict high-resolution inundation over long periods of time while only needing to model the domain at a high-resolution for a short training period, greatly reducing the computational cost.

Outside of the spatial training domain, the spatial ablation RF-PF model had an accuracy of 86.4% (F1 score of 0.75). Accuracy further de­ graded in temporally-variable cells excluded from training, which were predicted with 75.3% accuracy (F1 score of 0.63). While this is a de­ cline from the accuracy in locations included in the training data, this methodology is still more accurate than assuming the 1 km hydrologic model was accurate at the 100 m resolution. Further research should be done to see if higher spatial coverage in training data or additional input variables are able to increase the accuracy of this methodology in un­ seen locations as well as to test the transferability of this methodology between watersheds. This methodology could also be combined with satellite-based training data to increase the spatial coverage of training data without the computational cost of high-resolution modeling.

This study demonstrates that the combination of coarse physicsbased modeling and the use of machine learning methods to downscale the modeled inundation area can emulate high-resolution physics-based modeling at a much lower computational expense with little decrease in accuracy. This hybrid methodology could be a key strategy in predicting high-resolution inundation at spatial and temporal scales which were not previously feasible due to the computational demand of high-resolution modeling.
